name: Chapter 11: Thermodynamics
description: Zeroth law, internal energy, heat and work, first law, Cp − Cv, state variables, isothermal and adiabatic processes, second law, Carnot engine

cards.term: What was the caloric theory of heat?
cards.definition: Heat as an invisible fluid ("caloric") filling the pores of matter, flowing until "caloric levels" equalised

cards.term: How did Count Rumford (1798) disprove caloric theory?
cards.definition:
Boring a cannon produced heat that depended on the work done (by horses), not on the drill’s sharpness.
So heat is a form of energy

cards.term: Thermodynamics vs mechanics?
cards.definition: Mechanics: motion of the body as a whole. Thermodynamics: the internal macroscopic state (P, V, T, U) — a bullet is not hotter because it is fast

cards.term: Is thermodynamics a microscopic or macroscopic science?
cards.definition: Macroscopic: it uses bulk variables (P, V, T, mass, composition) and ignores molecules

cards.term: Thermodynamic equilibrium vs mechanical equilibrium?
cards.definition: Thermodynamic: macroscopic variables do not change with time. Mechanical: net force and torque are zero

cards.term: Adiabatic wall vs diathermic wall?
cards.definition: Adiabatic: insulating, no heat flow. Diathermic: conducting, heat flows until thermal equilibrium

cards.text: Zeroth law: two systems in thermal equilibrium with a {{c1::third system}} separately are in thermal equilibrium with {{c2::each other}}.

cards.term: What concept does the zeroth law define?
cards.definition: Temperature: the quantity that is equal for systems in thermal equilibrium

cards.term: Who formulated the zeroth law, and why is it called "zeroth"?
cards.definition: R. H. Fowler (1931), after the first and second laws were already numbered; it is logically more basic

cards.term: Define internal energy.
cards.definition:
Sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies in the frame where the centre of mass is at rest.
It excludes the KE of the body as a whole

cards.term: Is internal energy a state variable? Heat? Work?
cards.definition: U: yes (depends only on the state). Heat and work: no — they are energy in transit and depend on the path

cards.term: Heat vs work as ways to change U?
cards.definition: Heat: transfer due to a temperature difference. Work: transfer by other means (e.g. moving a piston)

cards.term: Why is "a gas has a certain amount of heat" meaningless?
cards.definition: Heat is energy in transit, not a property of a state; the state has internal energy

cards.term: For an ideal gas, U depends on…?
cards.definition: Temperature only (no intermolecular forces)

cards.term: State the first law of thermodynamics.
cards.definition: \[\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W\]heat supplied = rise in internal energy + work done by the system

cards.term: First law sign conventions
cards.definition: Heat absorbed by the system: ΔQ > 0; Heat released: ΔQ < 0; Work done by the system (expansion): ΔW > 0; Work done on the system (compression): ΔW < 0

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

Sign?

Heat absorbed by the system?
Heat released?

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Sign convention (NCERT)

Sign?

Heat absorbed by the systemΔQ > 0
Heat releasedΔQ < 0
Work done by the system (expansion)ΔW > 0
Work done on the system (compression)ΔW < 0

Chemistry books often write ΔU = q + w with w = work done ON the system — same physics, different sign.

cards.term: The first law is really the law of…?
cards.definition: Conservation of energy, including heat and work exchanges

cards.term: Which combination of Q and W is path independent?
cards.definition: \[\Delta Q - \Delta W = \Delta U\]because U is a state variable (Q and W separately depend on the path)

cards.term: Work done by a gas against constant pressure?
cards.definition: \[\Delta W = P\,\Delta V\]in general, W = ∫P dV = area under the P–V curve

cards.term: Internal energy change on boiling water

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
11.5 · boiling 1 g of water

Find the missing step.

L = 2256 J/g; 1 g of water: 1 cm³ as liquid, 1671 cm³ as steam, at 1 atm. ΔU?
  1. ΔQ = 2256 J
  2. ΔW = P(V_g − V_l) = 1.013 × 10⁵ × 1670 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 169 J
  3. ?
  4. = ≈ 2087 J: most heat goes into internal energy
advancedHtml.backHtml:
11.5 · boiling 1 g of water

Find the missing step.

L = 2256 J/g; 1 g of water: 1 cm³ as liquid, 1671 cm³ as steam, at 1 atm. ΔU?
  1. ΔQ = 2256 J
  2. ΔW = P(V_g − V_l) = 1.013 × 10⁵ × 1670 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 169 J
  3. ΔU = ΔQ − ΔW
  4. = ≈ 2087 J: most heat goes into internal energy

cards.term: Exercise 11.7: heater supplies 100 W; system does work at 75 J/s. Rate of rise of U?
cards.definition: 25 W

cards.term: Exercise 11.5: A → B adiabatically needs 22.3 J of work on the gas. Via another path the gas absorbs 9.35 cal. Work done by the gas then?
cards.definition: ΔU = +22.3 J (same for any path); W = Q − ΔU = 39.2 − 22.3 = 16.9 J

cards.term: Molar specific heat of solids (Dulong–Petit)?
cards.definition: \[C \approx 3R \approx 25\]J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹: each atom is a 3D oscillator with energy 3kT

cards.term: Which solid in Table 11.1 breaks the 3R rule?
cards.definition: Carbon (6.1 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); the rule also fails at low temperatures

cards.term: Define the calorie precisely. 1 cal in joules?
cards.definition: Heat to raise 1 g of water from 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C; 1 cal = 4.186 J

cards.term: Why is "mechanical equivalent of heat" now superfluous?
cards.definition: Heat and work are both energy measured in joules; 4.186 J/cal is only a unit conversion

cards.term: Mayer’s relation for an ideal gas?
Proof of Mayer’s relation
cards.definition: At constant P the extra heat does work PΔV = RΔT per mole, so Cp − Cv = R

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
11.6 · proof of Cp − Cv = R

Find the missing step.

Prove Cp − Cv = R for one mole of an ideal gas.
  1. ΔQ = ΔU + PΔV
  2. Constant V: Cv = ΔU/ΔT
  3. ?
  4. So Cp − Cv = R
advancedHtml.backHtml:
11.6 · proof of Cp − Cv = R

Find the missing step.

Prove Cp − Cv = R for one mole of an ideal gas.
  1. ΔQ = ΔU + PΔV
  2. Constant V: Cv = ΔU/ΔT
  3. Constant P: Cp = ΔU/ΔT + P(ΔV/ΔT); PV = RT gives P ΔV/ΔT = R
  4. So Cp − Cv = R

cards.term: Why is Cp > Cv?
cards.definition: At constant pressure part of the heat does work (expansion); at constant volume all of it raises U

cards.term: Exercise 11.2: heat to raise 20 g of nitrogen by 45 °C at constant pressure?
cards.definition: μ = 20/28 mol, Cp = 7R/2 → Q ≈ 933 J

cards.term: Exercise 11.3(a): why don’t two bodies in contact settle at (T₁ + T₂)/2?
cards.definition: Only if their heat capacities are equal; in general the final temperature is weighted by ms

cards.term: Exercise 11.3(b): why should a coolant have high specific heat?
cards.definition: It absorbs a lot of heat with only a small rise in its temperature

cards.term: Exercise 11.3(d): why is a harbour town’s climate milder than a desert town’s?
cards.definition: The sea’s high heat capacity (and humid air) smooths temperature changes

cards.term: What is an equation of state? Example?
cards.definition: A relation among state variables; for an ideal gas \( PV = \mu RT \) (only two of P, V, T independent)

cards.term: Can a gas in free expansion or an explosion be described by state variables?
cards.definition: No: it is not in equilibrium; P and T are not uniform

cards.term: Extensive vs intensive variables? Test?
cards.definition:
Divide the system in two:
variables that halve are extensive (U, V, mass)
variables that stay unchanged are intensive (P, T, ρ)

cards.term: Is ΔQ = ΔU + PΔV consistent in extensive/intensive terms?
cards.definition: Yes: every term is extensive (P × ΔV is intensive × extensive)

cards.term: What is an isotherm?
cards.definition: The P–V curve at fixed temperature

cards.term: What is a quasi-static process?
cards.definition:
An infinitely slow process.
The system stays in equilibrium, differing from the surroundings only infinitesimally in P and T

cards.term: Special thermodynamic processes (Table 11.2)
cards.definition: Isothermal: temperature; Isobaric: pressure; Isochoric: volume; Adiabatic: no heat flow (ΔQ = 0)

advancedHtml.backHtml:

What is kept fixed?

Isothermaltemperature
Isobaricpressure

cards.term: Identify the four processes starting from A on this P–V diagram.
cards.definition:
Horizontal: isobaric
vertical: isochoric
PV = const: isothermal
steeper PVᵞ = const: adiabatic

cards.term: Isothermal process of an ideal gas: relation, ΔU, work?
cards.definition: PV = constant (Boyle); ΔU = 0;\[Q = W = \mu RT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\]

cards.term: Isothermal expansion vs compression: heat?
cards.definition: Expansion: gas absorbs heat and does work. Compression: work is done on it and it releases heat

cards.term: Adiabatic process of an ideal gas: relation?
cards.definition: \( PV^\gamma = constant \), γ = Cp/Cv; also \( TV^{\gamma-1} = constant \)

cards.term: Work done by an ideal gas in an adiabatic change?
cards.definition: \[W = \dfrac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{\mu R(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}\]

cards.term: Adiabatic expansion: what happens to temperature? Compression?
cards.definition: Expansion: work comes from U → gas cools. Compression: gas heats up (e.g. a bicycle pump)

cards.term: Why is an adiabat steeper than an isotherm on a P–V graph?
cards.definition: Slope: isotherm −P/V, adiabat −γP/V (γ > 1)

cards.term: Isochoric process?
cards.definition: W = 0; all heat changes U:\[Q = \mu C_v\Delta T\]

cards.term: Isobaric process?
cards.definition: \[W = P(V_2 - V_1) = \mu R(T_2 - T_1)\]Q = μCₚΔT

cards.term: Cyclic process?
cards.definition: ΔU = 0, so net heat absorbed = net work done = area enclosed by the loop

cards.term: Exercise 11.4: 3 mol of H₂ compressed adiabatically to half its volume. Pressure factor?
cards.definition: \[2^{1.4} \approx\]2.64

cards.term: Exercise 11.6: gas in A expands freely into evacuated B (equal volumes, insulated). Final P, ΔU, ΔT?
cards.definition: P halves (0.5 atm); ΔU = 0, ΔT = 0 (ideal gas: Q = 0, W = 0)

cards.term: Exercise 11.6(d): do the intermediate states of free expansion lie on the P–V–T surface?
cards.definition: No: free expansion is rapid; intermediate states are not equilibrium states

cards.term: Exercise 11.3(c): why does tyre pressure rise while driving?
cards.definition: Friction heats the tyre air at nearly constant volume, so P rises

cards.term: Exercise 11.8: gas goes D → E linearly (600 → 300 N/m², 2 → 5 m³), then isobarically back E → F. Total work?
cards.definition: Area of triangle DEF = ½ × 3 × 300 = 450 J

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Exercise 11.8 refers to "Fig. (11.13)". Which figure?
cards.definition: Fig. 11.11

cards.term: Why is the first law not enough?
cards.definition:
Many energy-conserving events never happen (a book jumping up by cooling the table).
The second law forbids them

cards.text: Kelvin–Planck statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and its {{c1::complete conversion into work}}.
Clausius statement: no process is possible whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a {{c1::colder}} object to a {{c2::hotter}} object.

cards.term: What do the two statements rule out?
cards.definition:
A heat engine with efficiency 1
A refrigerator with infinite coefficient of performance
The two statements are equivalent

cards.term: Teacher addition: efficiency of a heat engine?
cards.definition: \[\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} = 1 - \dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}\]

cards.term: Teacher addition: coefficient of performance of a refrigerator?
cards.definition: \( \beta = \dfrac{Q_2}{W} = \dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1 - Q_2} \); for a Carnot fridge \( \dfrac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2} \)

cards.term: Define a reversible process.
cards.definition: One that can be turned back so that both system and surroundings return to their original states, with no change elsewhere

cards.term: Conditions for reversibility?
cards.definition: Quasi-static and no dissipative effects (friction, viscosity)

cards.term: Two main causes of irreversibility?
cards.definition: Passing through non-equilibrium states (free expansion, explosions) and dissipation (friction, viscosity)

cards.term: Examples of irreversible processes?
cards.definition: Heat flowing from a hot base to the rest of a vessel, free expansion, combustion, diffusion of leaking gas, stirring a liquid

cards.term: Example of a (nearly) reversible process?
cards.definition: Quasi-static isothermal expansion of an ideal gas with a frictionless piston

cards.term: Why must a reversible engine between two temperatures use isothermal and adiabatic steps?
cards.definition:
Heat must be exchanged with no finite temperature difference (isothermal).
Temperature must be changed without other reservoirs (adiabatic)

cards.text: Carnot cycle: {{c1::isothermal expansion}} at T₁ → {{c2::adiabatic expansion}} to T₂ → {{c3::isothermal compression}} at T₂ → {{c4::adiabatic compression}} back to T₁.

cards.term: Identify: which parts of the Carnot cycle absorb and reject heat?
cards.definition:
1 → 2 (isothermal at T₁) absorbs Q₁
3 → 4 (isothermal at T₂) rejects Q₂
the two adiabats exchange no heat

cards.term: Efficiency of a Carnot engine?
cards.definition: \[\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\](kelvin temperatures)

cards.term: Key relation in a Carnot cycle (used to define temperature)?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\]independent of the working substance

cards.term: State Carnot’s theorem.
cards.definition: (a) No engine between T₁ and T₂ is more efficient than a Carnot engine. (b) Carnot efficiency is independent of the working substance

cards.term: How is Carnot’s theorem proved?
cards.definition:
If an engine I beat a reversible engine R run as a refrigerator,
the pair would turn heat from one reservoir fully into work,
violating Kelvin–Planck

cards.term: Who first analysed the ideal heat engine?
cards.definition: Sadi Carnot, French engineer, 1824

cards.term: Teacher addition: Carnot engine between 500 K and 300 K. Efficiency?
cards.definition: 1 − 300/500 = 40 %

cards.term: Can a Carnot engine have 100 % efficiency?
cards.definition: Only if T₂ = 0 K, which is unattainable

cards.term: Work in thermodynamic processes
cards.definition: Isochoric: 0; Isobaric: P(V₂ − V₁); Isothermal: μRT ln(V₂/V₁); Adiabatic: (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1); Cyclic: area of the loop

cards.definition: J s⁻¹ m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹): H = KA ΔT/L needs a per-metre unit
